prompt: Why can a specialised accelerator do far more arithmetic per joule than a general-purpose CPU core built on the same process?

options.text: Its multipliers and adders use a fundamentally cheaper kind of transistor
options.explanation: The arithmetic units are built from the same kind of transistors. The saving comes from what surrounds the arithmetic, not the arithmetic itself.

options.text: In a CPU, fetching, decoding and scheduling each instruction and moving its operands cost far more energy than the operation; an accelerator strips most of that out
options.explanation: Correct. A multiply costs a few picojoules, but instruction overhead and data movement (especially to DRAM) cost tens to hundreds. Accelerators amortise or remove that overhead.

options.text: Accelerators run at much higher clock speeds
options.explanation: Usually the opposite: the first TPU ran at 700 MHz and FPGAs at a few hundred MHz. They win on work per cycle and per joule, not clock speed.

options.text: Accelerators do not need memory, so they avoid DRAM entirely
options.explanation: They still need memory; the TPU read weights from DDR3 and later HBM. They reduce how often each value is fetched, but cannot avoid fetching it.

workedExample:
Compare where the energy goes for one useful operation.

1. On a CPU, one FP multiply is a few pJ.
2. Around it: instruction fetch from the I-cache, decode, rename, scheduling, register-file reads and writes. Together these dwarf the multiply.
3. If the operand comes from DRAM, that read costs hundreds of pJ.

An accelerator attacks steps 2 and 3: a GPU issues one instruction for 32 lanes, a systolic array has no per-operation instruction at all, and each operand fetched is reused many times. Same transistors, far less overhead.

link.title: In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a TPU (Jouppi et al., 2017)

prompt: Which device has **no instruction stream** at all, yet can be reconfigured after manufacture to implement a different circuit?

options.text: A GPU
options.explanation: A GPU fetches and decodes instructions; it just shares each one across a warp of threads.

options.text: An ASIC
options.explanation: An ASIC also has no instruction stream for its fixed function, but its circuit is fixed in silicon and cannot be rewired.

options.text: An FPGA
options.explanation: Correct. Its LUTs, flip-flops, DSP blocks and routing are configured by a bitstream, so the circuit is the program, and a new bitstream gives a new circuit.

options.text: A CPU with a large instruction cache
options.explanation: A big I-cache makes fetching cheaper but the CPU is still driven by an instruction stream.

workedExample:
Sort the devices with two questions.

| Device | Instructions? | Rewirable? |
|---|---|---|
| CPU | yes | no |
| GPU | yes, per warp | no |
| FPGA | no | yes |
| ASIC | no | no |

Only the FPGA answers "no, yes". That is why it sits between the GPU and the ASIC on the flexibility–efficiency spectrum.

prompt: A hypothetical accelerator has a 128 × 128 array of multiply-accumulate (MAC) units clocked at 1 GHz. Counting each MAC as two operations, what is its peak throughput?

options.text: About 16 TOPS
options.explanation: This counts each MAC as one operation. A MAC is a multiply and an add, so it is two.

options.text: About 256 GOPS
options.explanation: This uses 128 × 2 instead of 128 × 128: it counts one row of the array, not the whole grid.

options.text: About 65 TOPS
options.explanation: This uses a 256 × 256 array (65,536 MACs) counted once per cycle. The array here is 128 × 128.

options.text: About 33 TOPS
options.explanation: Correct. 16,384 MACs × 2 ops × 10⁹ cycles/s ≈ 32.8 × 10¹² ops/s.

workedExample:
Work it out the same way as the TPU v1 figure in the lesson:

```
MACs   = 128 x 128     = 16,384
ops    = 16,384 x 2    = 32,768/cyc
peak   = 32,768 x 1e9  ~ 32.8 TOPS
```

For comparison, TPU v1 was 65,536 MACs × 2 × 700 MHz ≈ 92 TOPS. Peak assumes every MAC is busy every cycle, which needs big enough matrices and enough memory bandwidth.

prompt: Use the lesson's output-stationary systolic array, where at cycle `t` PE(i, j) multiplies `A[i][k] * B[k][j]` with `k = t - i - j` (if `0 <= k < n`). With n = 4, what does PE(1, 2) compute at cycle t = 4?

options.explanation: Correct. k = 4 − 1 − 2 = 1, so PE(1, 2) multiplies A[1][1] by B[1][2] and adds it to C[1][2].
This uses k = t. Row i is delayed by i cycles and column j by j cycles, so you must subtract i + j.

options.text: Nothing; it is idle at cycle 4
options.explanation: It is idle only when k falls outside 0..3. Here k = 1, which is valid.
This uses k = j, as if the PE's column index picked the term. The term index depends on the cycle and both delays.

workedExample:
1. Row 1 of A enters 1 cycle late; column 2 of B enters 2 cycles late.
2. So at cycle t the values meeting at PE(1, 2) have index k = t − 1 − 2.
3. At t = 4, k = 1: the PE computes A[1][1] × B[1][2].

PE(1, 2) is active for k = 0..3, i.e. cycles 3 to 6. The whole 4 × 4 multiply finishes after 3n − 2 = 10 cycles (t = 0..9), with PE(3, 3) doing its last MAC at t = 9.

prompt: From TPU v2 onwards Google used **bfloat16** for training rather than IEEE FP16. What is the main reason?

options.text: bfloat16 has more mantissa bits, so it is more precise than FP16
options.explanation: The reverse: bfloat16 has 7 mantissa bits against FP16's 10. It is *less* precise.

options.text: bfloat16 keeps FP32's 8-bit exponent, so it covers the same range and gradients rarely overflow or underflow, at half FP32's storage
options.explanation: Correct. Training is more sensitive to range than to the last few bits of precision, and converting from FP32 is just truncating the mantissa.

options.text: bfloat16 is an integer format, so it needs no floating-point hardware
options.explanation: bfloat16 is a floating-point format: sign, exponent and mantissa. Integer formats like int8 were what TPU v1 used for inference.

options.text: bfloat16 uses 8 bits, so twice as many values fit in memory as FP16
options.explanation: bfloat16 is 16 bits, the same size as FP16. It splits those bits differently.

workedExample:
Lay out the bits:

```
          sign exp mantissa
FP32       1    8    23
FP16       1    5    10
bfloat16   1    8     7
```

FP16's 5-bit exponent tops out around 65,504, and small gradients underflow, which is why FP16 training needs loss scaling. bfloat16 has FP32's range, so models can usually train without it. The cost is precision, which is why accumulation is typically done in FP32.

prompt: A job spends 60% of its time on matrix multiplies. Moving them to an accelerator makes them 20× faster, but copying data to and from the device adds time equal to 10% of the original runtime. What is the overall speed-up?

options.text: About 20×
options.explanation: Only 60% of the work gets the 20× speed-up. The other 40% and the transfer time do not shrink.

options.text: About 2.3×
options.explanation: This is Amdahl's law without the transfer cost: 1 / (0.4 + 0.03) ≈ 2.33. The copies add another 0.1.

options.text: About 1.9×
options.explanation: Correct. New time = 0.4 + 0.6/20 + 0.1 = 0.53 of the original, so the speed-up is 1 / 0.53 ≈ 1.89×.

options.text: About 1.1×
options.explanation: This would follow if the transfer cost 40% or so of the runtime. At 10% the offload is still clearly worthwhile.

workedExample:
Normalise the original runtime to 1.

```
not offloaded   0.40
matmul 0.6/20   0.03
transfers       0.10
----------------------
new total       0.53
speed-up 1/0.53 ~ 1.89x
```

Two lessons: Amdahl caps you at 1/0.4 = 2.5× however fast the accelerator is, and data movement eats into that. Keeping data on the device across many operations removes the 0.10.

prompt: Which of these are good fits for an **FPGA**? Select all that apply.

options.text: A trading system that must turn a market-data packet into an order with deterministic, sub-microsecond latency
options.explanation: Good fit. A custom pipeline processes each packet in a fixed number of cycles, with no OS, caches or branch mispredictions adding jitter.

options.text: Video decoding in a phone that will ship in hundreds of millions of units
options.explanation: Poor fit. At that volume a fixed ASIC block pays back its NRE and wins on power, area and unit cost.

options.text: Prototyping and verifying a new chip design before committing to masks
options.explanation: Good fit. FPGAs let engineers run the real logic at useful speed and fix bugs cheaply before tape-out.

options.text: A web application's business logic that changes every week
options.explanation: Poor fit. It is branchy, irregular code with little data parallelism, and hours-long hardware builds would make weekly changes painful. A CPU is the right tool.

options.text: Line-rate packet processing in cloud servers, as in Microsoft's Catapult and Azure Accelerated Networking
options.explanation: Good fit. A new packet every cycle through a parallel pipeline, and the logic can be updated in the field as protocols evolve.

workedExample:
FPGAs win when you need custom, deeply pipelined hardware but cannot justify (or cannot wait for) an ASIC.

| Workload | Verdict | Why |
|---|---|---|
| HFT | FPGA | fixed latency |
| phone video | ASIC | huge volume |
| prototyping | FPGA | reconfigurable |
| web logic | CPU | irregular |
| cloud packets | FPGA | line rate |

Ask: is the work regular enough for a pipeline, and is the volume too low (or the logic too changeable) for an ASIC?

prompt: In an n × n systolic array, why does each value fetched from memory support about n multiply-accumulates?

options.text: The value is cached in an L1 cache beside every PE, so later reads are cheap
options.explanation: Systolic PEs have no caches. Reuse comes from passing values between neighbours, not from caching them.

options.text: Each PE fetches its own copy of the value from memory, but memory is very fast
options.explanation: That is exactly what the design avoids. If every PE fetched its own operands, bandwidth would limit the array to a tiny fraction of peak.

options.text: The value is compressed so it takes 1/n of the bandwidth
options.explanation: Compression is not part of the systolic idea. The saving is reuse, not smaller values.

options.text: The value enters at one edge and is passed PE to PE along its row or column, so every PE it passes uses it once
options.explanation: Correct. One fetch, n uses. With n = 256 that is 256 MACs per value read from the buffer.

workedExample:
Follow one element of A, say A[2][0], through a 4 × 4 output-stationary array.

1. It enters row 2 at the left edge.
2. Each cycle it moves one PE right: PE(2,0), PE(2,1), PE(2,2), PE(2,3).
3. Each of those PEs multiplies it by a different B value.

So one read feeds 4 MACs; for a 256-wide array, 256. Short neighbour-to-neighbour wires replace register-file and cache accesses, which is where the energy saving comes from.

prompt: An FPGA packet pipeline runs at 300 MHz and accepts one packet per cycle. A server has 8 CPU cores at 3 GHz, each needing about 200 cycles per packet. Roughly how do their packet rates compare?

options.text: The CPU is 10× faster because its clock is 10× higher
options.explanation: Clock speed alone says nothing about throughput. The FPGA finishes one packet per cycle; each CPU core needs 200 cycles per packet.

options.text: The FPGA handles about 300 M packets/s, the CPU about 120 M packets/s, so the FPGA is about 2.5× faster
They are equal, because both process 8 packets at once
options.explanation: The FPGA pipeline holds many packets in flight (one per stage), not 8, and the CPU's rate depends on cycles per packet.

options.text: The FPGA is 200× faster
options.explanation: This compares one packet per cycle against 200 cycles per packet but forgets the CPU's 10× higher clock and its 8 cores.

workedExample:
Compute throughput for each.

```
FPGA: 300e6 cyc/s x 1 pkt/cyc
    = 300 M pkt/s
CPU core: 3e9 / 200 = 15 M pkt/s
CPU x 8 cores        = 120 M pkt/s
ratio 300 / 120      = 2.5x
```

The FPGA also wins on latency predictability: every packet takes the same number of pipeline stages, while CPU latency varies with cache misses, interrupts and scheduling.

prompt: An inference server fills its accelerator efficiently only with batches of 64. Requests arrive steadily at 1,000 per second, and the server waits for a full batch before running. What is the **longest** extra queuing delay a request suffers from batching?

options.text: About 1 ms
options.explanation: That is the gap between two arrivals. The first request of a batch waits for the next 63 to arrive.

options.text: About 32 ms
options.explanation: That is roughly the *average* wait across a batch (from 63 ms for the first request down to 0 for the last). The question asks for the worst case.

options.text: About 64 seconds
options.explanation: This confuses the batch size with seconds. At 1,000 requests per second, 64 requests arrive in 64 ms.

options.text: About 63 ms
options.explanation: Correct. The first request in a batch waits while 63 more arrive, at 1 ms apart.

workedExample:
1. Arrivals are 1 / 1,000 s = 1 ms apart.
2. The first request of a batch arrives at t = 0; the 64th at t = 63 ms.
3. The batch launches at 63 ms, so the first request waited 63 ms before any compute.

Average wait is about 31.5 ms. Real servers cap this with a timeout ("run whatever we have after 5 ms"), trading accelerator utilisation for latency. At low traffic, the batch is small and the expensive chip is mostly idle.

prompt: TPU v1 peaks at about 92 TOPS but reads weights from DRAM at about 34 GB/s. In a fully connected layer, each int8 weight (1 byte) is used once per example in the batch, as one MAC (2 ops). Ignoring activations, roughly what batch size is needed before the layer stops being limited by weight bandwidth?

options.text: About 1,350
options.explanation: Correct. The chip needs 92 × 10¹² / 34 × 10⁹ ≈ 2,700 ops per weight byte; with 2 ops per weight per example, that is a batch of about 1,350.

options.text: About 2,700
options.explanation: 2,700 is the ops per byte needed, but each example contributes 2 ops (a multiply and an add) per weight byte, so you need half as many examples.

options.text: About 64
options.explanation: At batch 64 the layer does only 128 ops per weight byte, so it can reach about 34 × 10⁹ × 128 ≈ 4.4 TOPS, under 5% of peak.

options.text: Batch size does not matter; the layer is always compute-bound on a TPU
options.explanation: The TPU paper found several production networks were memory-bound for exactly this reason: weight reuse depends on batch size.

workedExample:
This is a roofline calculation (next lesson).

```
needed = peak / bandwidth
       = 92e12 / 34e9
       ~ 2,700 ops per byte
layer  = 2 ops x B per weight byte
2B = 2,700  ->  B ~ 1,350
```

Below that, throughput is about 34 GB/s × 2B ops/byte. At B = 200 that is 13.6 TOPS, around 15% of peak. This is why later TPUs moved to HBM with far higher bandwidth.

link.title: In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a TPU (Jouppi et al., 2017)

prompt: A start-up is deciding between building an ASIC and shipping on FPGAs for a new compression algorithm. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: An ASIC at an advanced node carries millions of dollars of up-front NRE (design, verification, masks) and a year or more of lead time
options.explanation: True. That fixed cost only pays back at high volume.

options.text: If the algorithm changes after tape-out, the ASIC's fixed logic cannot be updated, while an FPGA can load a new bitstream
options.explanation: True. Field reconfigurability is the FPGA's main advantage over an ASIC.

options.text: An FPGA will always beat an ASIC on performance per watt, because it is reconfigurable
options.explanation: False. Reconfigurability costs area, routing and clock speed. For a fixed function at volume, an ASIC is more efficient.

options.text: FPGAs typically clock at a few hundred MHz, so the design must get its speed from wide, deep pipelines
options.explanation: True. FPGAs make up for low clocks with many operations in parallel per cycle.

options.text: Choosing an FPGA removes the need for hardware design skills, because you program it like a CPU
options.explanation: False. You still design a circuit in Verilog, VHDL or HLS, then synthesise, place and route it, which can take hours.

workedExample:
Weigh the trade-off along the spectrum.

| Factor | FPGA | ASIC |
|---|---|---|
| Up-front cost | low | very high |
| Unit cost at volume | higher | lower |
| Perf/watt | good | best |
| Changeable later | yes | no |

A common path is to ship on FPGAs while the algorithm settles and volumes are low, then move to an ASIC once both are stable.
